chapter_theme: Strength is not a fixed quantity but depends on when it is used. The chapter's real teaching is about waiting: holding back, even bowing and hiding one's anger, then striking without hesitation when the moment comes. Its stance is cold and tactical.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar's divisions: the distinction of time (481), its fruits (482-484), what to do when the time has not come (485-488), and what to do when it has (489), with the heron giving both (490).

481.reading: By day the crow beats the owl; kings who would win a contest need the right time.
481.nuance: The image makes strength relational, as the same two birds reverse by night, a symmetry Manakkudavar makes explicit. Parimelazhagar's definition of time is unexpectedly concrete: weather that lets an army travel without disease and with food and water.

482.reading: Acting in accord with the season is the rope that binds fortune so that it doesn't leave.
482.nuance: A rope only makes sense for something that tends to run. Parimelazhagar draws this from தீராமை: fortune's nature is to leave. Kalaignar takes திருவினை differently, as the success of a good deed, but the older commentators read wealth.

483.reading: Are there things said to be hard, if one acts with the right means and knows the time?
483.nuance: Parimelazhagar notes that கருவியான் is there to say that even with the means, time is still needed: the tools don't make timing unnecessary.

484.reading: Even the world will come to hand if one thinks of the time and acts by the place.
484.nuance: This verse joins time and place and forms a bridge into the next chapter. The promise is grand, and the chapter's next verse immediately makes the same ambition the reason for doing nothing yet.

485.reading: Those who have their mind on the world wait, unshaken, with their mind on the time.
485.nuance: Greater ambition means more waiting, not less. Parimelazhagar adds that this applies even if one's strength is already superior, and identifies இருப்பு as a recognised policy, one of six, the opposite of marching out. கலங்காது could go with either the waiting or the aim.

486.reading: The holding back of the person of energy is like a fighting ram drawing back in order to charge.
486.nuance: It reframes restraint as part of attack, so ஒடுக்கம் doesn't signal a lack of ஊக்கம். Kalaignar adds that this is silence in the face of cruelty and that it isn't from fear, which the verse doesn't say.

487.reading: The bright don't flare up outwardly at once; watching the time, they burn within.
487.nuance: The anger isn't removed, only stored. Parimelazhagar gives the unusual reason that it must continue within: if it died away, one could not later stop the offender. Anger here is a resource.

488.reading: Seeing those who would harm you, bear them; when you see their final limit, the head goes down.
488.nuance: The verse doesn't say what is to be carried or whose head falls. Manakkudavar's தலையினாற் சுமக்க is the literal image behind Parimelazhagar's reading: carry them on the head, then tip them off.

positions.position: Actually bow to the enemy until his time comes. Your submission makes him careless, and that is why his head falls.
positions.quote: பணியவே, அக்காலம் வந்திறும் வழி அவர் தகைவின்றி இறுவர்.

positions.position: Bear one's own feelings of enmity patiently, and the enemy falls by himself.
positions.quote: தங்களின் பகையுணர்வைப் பொறுமையுடன் தாங்கிக் கொள்ள வேண்டும்.

489.reading: When what is hard to get has come, do at that very point what is hard to do.
489.nuance: The double அரிய pairs them: rare time, rare deed. Parimelazhagar makes the best observation on அந்நிலையே: the moment won't stay. All the patience of the preceding verses exists for this one instant.

490.reading: When it is the season to fold up, be like the heron; when the moment is right, be like its strike.
490.nuance: One image holds both modes, and the verse compares the person first to the bird and then only to the bird's stab. Parimelazhagar notes that the heron looks as though lifeless while it waits, which adds a touch of menace.

links.note: 376 says what isn't yours won't stay however you guard it. 482 offers timing as the rope that keeps fortune from leaving. One denies that wealth can be held by care, the other names the means of holding it.

303 says to forget anger toward anyone, because evil is born of it. 487 keeps anger alive in secret until it can be used. The Aram book treats anger as something to give up, while the Porul book treats it as something to store.
488 advises bowing to an enemy until he can be struck. 828 warns that a weapon is hidden in an enemy's folded hands. The Kural gives the technique and the defence against it, from either side.
471 says act after weighing strengths. Parimelazhagar's 485 says that even with greater strength, wait for the time. So a favourable reckoning from 471 still isn't enough.

source_issues: 487: Manakkudavar's மனமொப்பர் and ஒப்புப் பொறாமையால் are obscure and may be corrupt, so I did not use them.
